title: Proposition
body_md: Let $g \in G$. If $\mathrm{NMI}(f(X), f(\rho(g)X)) < 1$, then $f$ is not $G$-equivariant at $g$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Proof by contrapositive.
    Let $X$ be a random variable taking values in $\mathcal{X}$ and let $f\colon \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$ be $G$-equivariant, so that $f(\rho_x(g)x) = \rho_y(g)f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathcal{X}$. 
    Define the random variables $Y := f(X)$, and $Y' := f(\rho_x(g)X)$.
    By equivariance, $Y' = \rho_y(g)Y$, and since $\rho_y(g)$ is a group action and hence invertible, $Y = \rho_y(g)^{-1}Y'$. Each of $Y$ and $Y'$ is therefore a deterministic function of the other, so $H(Y \mid Y') = H(Y' \mid Y) = 0$, and by \Cref{lemma:mutual-determinism},
    $\mathrm{NMI}(Y, Y') = \mathrm{NMI}(f(X), f(\rho_x(g)X)) = 1$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $g \in G$. Assume $\rho_\mathbf{Y}(g)$ is orthogonal. Also assume orthogonally invariant kernels $K$ that use the same feature map. (For example, linear or RBF kernels).
    If $\mathrm{CKA}(K_{f(\mathbf{X})}, K_{f(\rho_\mathbf{X}(g)\mathbf{X})}) < 1$,  
    the function $f$ is not $G$-equivariant at $g$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Proof by contrapositive.
    Assume $f\colon \mathbf{X} \rightarrow \mathbf{Y}$ is $G$-equivariant and $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are sets. 
    Let $\mathbf{Y} := f(\mathbf{X})$ and $\mathbf{Y}' := f(\rho_\mathbf{X}(g)\mathbf{X})$. 
    Since $f$ is $G$-equivariant, there exists an invertible orthogonal map $\rho_\mathbf{Y}(g)$ such that $\mathbf{Y}' =\rho_\mathbf{Y}(g)\mathbf{Y}$. 
    Following our two assumptions, $\rho_\mathbf{Y}(g)$ is orthogonal and our kernel functions $K_\mathbf{Y}$ and $K_{\mathbf{Y}'}$ are orthogonally invariant.
    Therefore $K_\mathbf{Y} = \langle \theta(y), \theta(y') \rangle = \langle \theta(\rho_y(g)y), \theta(\rho_y(g)y') \rangle = K_{\mathbf{Y}'}$.
    By \cref{lemma:extremal-cka-proprotional-gram-matrices}, $\mathrm{CKA}(K_\mathbf{Y}, K_{\mathbf{Y}'}) = 1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By definition of mutual information, $I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X)$, therefore $2I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - (H(X|Y) + H(Y|X))$. 
    
    If $\mathrm{NMI}(X, Y) = 1$, then by definition $\frac{2I(X;Y)}{H(X) + H(Y)} = \frac{H(X) + H(Y) - (H(X|Y) + H(Y|X))}{H(X) + H(Y)} = 1 - \frac{H(X|Y) + H(Y|X)}{H(X) + H(Y)} = 1$, so $ \frac{H(X|Y) + H(Y|X)}{H(X) + H(Y)} = 0$ which requires $H(X|Y) + H(Y|X) = 0$

    If $H(X|Y) = H(Y|X) = 0$, then $2I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - (H(X|Y) + H(Y|X)) = H(X) + H(Y)$. Therefore $\mathrm{NMI}(X, Y)=1$.

label: lemma:extremal-cka-proportional-gram-matrices
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:extremal-cka-proportional-gram-matrices}
    Under the nondegeneracy assumption $\tilde{X}\neq 0$ and $\tilde{Y}\neq 0$,
    \[
    \mathrm{CKA}(K_X, K_Y) = 1 \iff \tilde{X} = c\,\tilde{Y} \text{ for some } c > 0,
    \]
    where $\tilde{X} = HK_XH$ and $\tilde{Y} = HK_YH$ are the centered Gram matrices.
    \label{lemma:extremal-cka-proprotional-gram-matrices}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Vectorize the centered Gram matrices and treat them as elements of
    $\mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ with the Frobenius inner product
    $\langle A, B \rangle_F = \operatorname{tr}(A^{\top}B)$. By definition, CKA is the
    cosine of the angle between them:
    $\mathrm{CKA}(K_\mathbf{X}, K_\mathbf{Y}) = \dfrac{\langle \tilde{X}, \tilde{Y} \rangle_F}{\|\tilde{X}\|_F\,\|\tilde{Y}\|_F}$.
    
    By the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality,
    $|\langle \tilde{X}, \tilde{Y} \rangle_F| \leq \|\tilde{X}\|_F\,\|\tilde{Y}\|_F$,
    so $\mathrm{CKA} \in [-1, 1]$, with equality $|\mathrm{CKA}| = 1$ iff $\tilde{X}$
    and $\tilde{Y}$ are linearly dependent, i.e.\ $\tilde{X} = c\,\tilde{Y}$ for some
    $c \neq 0$ (nonzero by nondegeneracy).
    
    Since $K_\mathbf{X}, K_\mathbf{Y}$ are Gram matrices they are positive semidefinite, and centering
    preserves this, so
    $\langle \tilde{X}, \tilde{Y} \rangle_F = \operatorname{tr}(\tilde{X}\tilde{Y})
    = \operatorname{tr}\!\big(\tilde{X}^{1/2}\tilde{Y}\,\tilde{X}^{1/2}\big) \geq 0$.
    Hence the numerator is nonnegative and $\mathrm{CKA} \in [0, 1]$.
    
    Combining the two: $\mathrm{CKA} = 1$ forces the Cauchy--Schwarz equality
    $\tilde{X} = c\,\tilde{Y}$ together with $\langle \tilde{X}, \tilde{Y} \rangle_F \ge 0$.
    Substituting gives $\langle \tilde{X}, \tilde{Y} \rangle_F = c\,\|\tilde{Y}\|_F^2$,
    which is nonnegative only when $c > 0$. Conversely, if $\tilde{X} = c\,\tilde{Y}$
    with $c > 0$, direct substitution yields $\mathrm{CKA} = 1$.
